item.title: bicep-deploy vs bicep-action: A Tool or a Workflow?
item.description:
I maintain innofactororg/bicep-action, so I should say up front that I am not a neutral party. I am also the person who most needs this comparison to be honest, because every time someone evaluates bicep-action for a new estate, the first question is the obvious one: why not just use Microsoft’s?

Microsoft’s answer to “how do I deploy Bicep from a pipeline” is Azure/bicep-deploy, published as the azure/bicep-deploy@v2 GitHub Action, with the same engine shipped to Azure DevOps as the BicepDeploy@0 task. It is official, MIT-licensed, actively developed, and its latest release, v2.5.0 at the end of October 2026, added what-if support for deployment stacks. If you need to deploy a Bicep file to Azure from CI, it does that, cleanly and with Microsoft behind it.

bicep-action answers a different question. It is not a deploy step; it is a deployment workflow. It plans every change in the pull request, posts the plan as a comment for people to review, runs quality gates, and deploys only the plan that was approved, on GitHub and Azure DevOps alike.

That distinction, a tool versus a workflow, explains almost every row in the grids below. Most of the time the right choice is obvious once you know which one you need. This post sets out what each does, where each is stronger, and where each falls short, using the current releases of both: azure/bicep-deploy v2.5.0 and BicepDeploy@0, and bicep-action v2026.11.13.

Two different shapes

Azure/bicep-deploy is a primitive. One step, one operation. You give it a type (deployment or deploymentStack), an operation (create, validate, whatIf, and for stacks delete), a scope, and your template and parameters. It compiles the Bicep, calls Azure Resource Manager through the Azure SDK for JavaScript, and writes the result to the log. Everything else about your pipeline, when it runs, who approves it, what happens to the what-if output, is yours to build around it.

Under the hood it is a TypeScript Node 24 action. The engine lives in a shared package, @azure/bicep-deploy-common, which the Azure Pipelines BicepDeploy@0 task also consumes, so both platforms get the same behaviour and the same input set. Authentication is separate: on GitHub you run azure/login first, and the action picks up the credential through a chained Azure credential; on Azure DevOps you pass a service connection.

bicep-action is a workflow. A plan action and a deploy action on GitHub, and a pipeline plus reusable stage templates on Azure DevOps, all running the same Bash scripts over the Azure CLI. The plan job builds, validates, runs the what-if, the delete gate, PSRule, a cost estimate and a snapshot check, then posts one comment on the pull request. The deploy job waits for an environment approval, deploys with the Bicep version and stack settings the plan used, and comments the result. Sign-in, provider registration and auto merge are part of it.

At a glance

Azure/bicep-deploy bicep-action
What it is A deploy/validate/what-if step A plan, review and deploy workflow
Maintainer Microsoft Innofactor (open source)
Licence MIT BSD 3-Clause
GitHub azure/bicep-deploy@v2 action plan and deploy composite actions
Azure DevOps BicepDeploy@0 task (same engine) Full pipeline and stage templates (same scripts)
Implementation TypeScript, Node 24, Azure SDK for JS Bash scripts over Azure CLI, Bicep CLI, jq
Runner OS Any runner that runs Node actions Linux (Bash) runners
Authentication azure/login (GitHub), service connection (Azure DevOps) Built in: OpenID Connect or secret (GitHub), service connection (Azure DevOps)
Where the what-if goes Job log, colour-formatted Pull request comment, logs artifact, and whatif-summary.json
Release model Semantic versions, v2 major tag Dated releases, v1 tag

Feature coverage

This is the grid most people want. “Build it yourself” means the capability is not in the tool but you can assemble it from the platform and your own scripts.

Capability Azure/bicep-deploy bicep-action
Standard deployments: resource group, subscription, management group, tenant Yes Yes
Deployment stacks: resource group, subscription, management group Yes Yes
What-if for standard deployments Yes Yes
What-if for stacks Yes (since v2.5.0) Yes
Validate Yes, with validation-level (provider, template, providerNoRbac) Yes (validate step)
.bicepparam and JSON parameter files Yes Yes
Inline parameters Yes (parameters input) No
Exclude change types from what-if Yes (what-if-exclude-change-types) No input; ignore and no-change results are left out of the comment
Pin the Bicep version Yes (bicep-version input) Automatic: the deploy uses the version the plan recorded
Template outputs as step outputs Yes, with masked-outputs No; the deploy action has no outputs
Sovereign clouds Yes (environment input) No input
Delete a stack Yes (operation: delete) No
What-if posted to the pull request Build it yourself Yes, one comment per plan
Deploy result posted to the pull request Build it yourself Yes
Approval before deploy Build it yourself with environments Built in, through environments
Deploy exactly what was planned Build it yourself (pass the same version and settings) Yes: Bicep version, mode and stack settings enforced
Approval list for stack deletes No Yes, delete gate with approved resource IDs
Fail on non-deterministic deletes No Yes, in delete modes
Policy and best-practice checks Build it yourself PSRule for Azure, optional
Cost estimate and budget gate Build it yourself Azure Cost Estimator, optional failing threshold
Snapshot drift check Build it yourself Automatic when a snapshot file is committed
Machine-readable what-if summary No whatif-summary.json (counts, IDs, deterministic, blocked)
Wait for a new subscription to become visible No Yes, retries that one error up to 30 minutes
Register resource providers before deploy No Yes, from the providers the plan found
Keep existing tag values (such as createdOn) No Yes, scoped to resource groups you name
Auto merge after deploy Build it yourself Yes (GitHub)
One run at a time per target Build it yourself Documented concurrency pattern in every example
Multi-environment examples Single-environment examples Test → production examples for both platforms

Deployment stacks, side by side

Stacks are where both projects have invested most, and where they differ in philosophy rather than coverage.

Stack option Azure/bicep-deploy bicep-action
Action on unmanaged resources Separate settings for resources, resource groups and management groups (delete or detach) One setting: detachAll (default), deleteResources, deleteAll
Deny settings mode none, denyDelete, denyWriteAndDelete none, denyDelete, denyWriteAndDelete
Deny settings excluded actions and principals Yes No
Deny settings on child scopes Yes No
Bypass the stack out-of-sync error Yes No
Stack description and tags Yes No
Deletes require an approval list No Yes
Re-check deletes immediately before deploy No Yes, in delete modes
Stack settings must match the plan No Yes

Microsoft exposes more of the stack API, and if you need deny-setting exclusions for a break-glass principal, or per-scope control of what gets deleted, bicep-action cannot express that today.

bicep-action, on the other hand, treats deletion as something that needs a reviewed commit. With action-on-unmanage-resources: delete in Microsoft’s action, removing a resource from the template deletes it on the next create. That is the documented, intended behaviour of a stack. Whether a human saw the what-if first depends entirely on how you built the pipeline around it. In bicep-action, a delete mode fails the plan unless every resource the stack would delete is listed by ID in an approved-deletes file, and fails it outright if Azure cannot determine every resource that might be deleted. The deploy job then runs that check again against the current state, because the plan may be hours old.

Strengths and weaknesses, honestly

Azure/bicep-deploy

Where it is stronger

  • It is Microsoft’s. Official support, the Bicep team’s own contributors, a Contributor Licence Agreement process, CodeQL and dependency automation. For organisations that only adopt vendor-supported tooling, that ends the discussion.
  • It is light and portable. A single Node step with no Azure CLI dependency, running on Linux, Windows or macOS runners, with the Bicep binary kept in the runner’s tool cache, so a self-hosted runner downloads each version once.
  • It exposes more of the API. Validation levels, what-if change-type filters, inline parameters, sovereign clouds, stack delete, and the full set of stack and deny-setting options.
  • Outputs flow on. Template outputs become step outputs, with masking for sensitive ones, so a later step can use the endpoint or resource ID the deployment produced.
  • Same engine on both platforms. The GitHub Action and the BicepDeploy@0 task share one package, so behaviour matches.
  • It composes. Because it does one thing, it fits into whatever pipeline design you already have.

Where it falls short

  • It is not a review workflow. The what-if goes to the job log. Getting it in front of a reviewer, gating the deploy on that review, and posting the result back are all left to you.
  • Plan and deploy are separate, unrelated runs. The examples validate on pull requests and create on push to main. Nothing records what the what-if run used, so nothing guarantees the deployment matches what anyone looked at, unless you pin the Bicep version and settings yourself in both places.
  • Deletes are not gated. Stacks will delete what you tell them to, with no approval list and no check for hidden deletes.
  • No quality gates. Policy checks, cost estimates and drift checks are outside its scope.
  • Young in places. Stack what-if arrived in v2.5.0 in October 2026, and the Azure DevOps task is still on major version 0.

bicep-action

Where it is stronger

  • The workflow is the product. Plan in the pull request, one comment with everything a reviewer needs, approval through the platform’s own environments, deployment of the approved plan, result posted back. Nothing to assemble.
  • Deploy matches plan as closely as ARM allows. The deploy installs the plan’s Bicep version, refuses different stack settings, and re-runs the delete gate. ARM has no saved plan file, so this is not a guarantee in the way Terraform’s is, but it closes the gaps a pipeline can close.
  • Safety by default. Deletes need a reviewed list of IDs, non-deterministic deletes fail, PSRule and a cost budget can fail the plan, and a committed snapshot catches template drift, including drift caused by a Bicep release.
  • Built for the details that break real pipelines. New subscriptions that are not visible yet, providers that are not registered, createdOn tags that should not be overwritten, masked values that garble a comment. Each feature exists because a production pipeline hit it.
  • Automation-ready. whatif-summary.json lets you auto-approve plans that are provably safe and route the rest to a person.
  • Same comments on GitHub and Azure DevOps, including multi-environment stage templates for Azure DevOps.

Where it falls short

  • It is not Microsoft’s. It is maintained by a partner team, and its priorities follow the production estates it runs in.
  • Linux and Bash only. It shells out to the Azure CLI, Bicep CLI, jq and Perl, so it needs a Linux runner and is slower to start than a single Node step.
  • Narrower API surface. No sovereign-cloud input, no inline parameters, no validation-level or what-if filters, no stack delete operation, and fewer stack and deny-setting options.
  • No deployment outputs. If a later step needs a value the template produced, you query Azure for it.
  • Opinionated. It assumes pull requests, environments and approvals. If your process deploys on push without review, most of what it does is in the way.
  • Azure DevOps downloads the scripts at run time from GitHub at the pinned release, so agents need to reach GitHub, and the template repository is referenced through a GitHub service connection.

Which one should you use?

Use Azure/bicep-deploy when you need a deployment step inside a pipeline you already own: a release pipeline with its own gates, a tool that consumes deployment outputs, a sovereign cloud, Windows runners, stack options bicep-action does not expose, or a policy that only vendor-supported tooling is allowed. It is also the right building block if you want to design your own review workflow from scratch.

Use bicep-action when what you want is the workflow: changes reviewed as plans in pull requests, deletes approved in commits, cost and policy checked before anyone deploys, and the same experience on GitHub and Azure DevOps. It is the one to pick when the question is not “how do I deploy this file” but “how do I stop anyone deploying something nobody looked at”.

They are not really competitors. bicep-deploy is a good primitive, and bicep-action is a workflow that today happens to be built on the Azure CLI rather than on that primitive. The gaps in the grids above run in opposite directions, which is usually a sign that two tools are solving different problems well. If you are standing at that fork, start from the question you are actually trying to answer, and the grid will tell you the rest.

Sources

  • Azure/bicep-deploy: README, action.yml, examples and release notes for v2.4.0 and v2.5.0
  • BicepDeployV0 task in microsoft/azure-pipelines-tasks
  • innofactororg/bicep-action: README, how it works, configuration reference and examples at v2026.11.13

item.title: Agents need an identity, and your IT department will say no
item.description:
Abstract

Everyone agrees AI agents should be treated like employees: their own identity, scoped permissions, an owner, monitoring and offboarding. Then you try to do it.

The agent on your laptop runs as you, because your machine is the security context. Your IT team rejects the application identity you ask for, because it doesn’t do MFA. Half your backends never see Entra ID at all, because they authenticate with personal access tokens. And the moment an agent can act on behalf of a user, “who owns this agent” quietly turns into “whose permissions does it have”.

This session is a practitioner’s account of doing this for real, using our own company as customer zero. We’ll cover where the identity breaks down, how an AI gateway can translate between Entra and legacy backends, and a simple governance model that holds up: an organisational ruleset for every agent, a versioned authorisation contract for each one, and runtime enforcement that stops an agent exceeding its contract even when it’s prompted to. Moving from “draft a message” to “send a message” is a permission change, not a new feature.

What attendees will learn:

  • Why agents default to the human’s identity, and what it takes to change that
  • Getting agent identities approved by security teams that currently say no
  • Using an AI gateway to bring non-Entra backends under the same control
  • A three-layer governance model: organisational rules, per-agent contracts, runtime enforcement
  • Why every change in an agent’s authority needs a version, an approver and evidence

Level: Intermediate–Advanced (300–400)

Audience: Security architects, identity and platform teams, AI and governance leads

item.title: Letting AI operate production Azure — what it gets wrong
item.description:
Abstract

Real failure stories from AI-assisted operations, each with the guardrail that fixed it:

  • an Azure GET can’t prove a property is settable (recommended four times off an empty read);
  • advising a change from a stale read in the middle of a cutover;
  • restating a verified fact until it’s wrong;
  • a disk caching change that hot-detached a production disk;
  • “a freeze is not a control”.

Plus the patterns that worked: subagents, cross-model review with gh copilot, and grep-verifying every HIGH finding. It’s honest, funny, and very MVP.

item.title: bicep-action: Plan, Review and Deploy Bicep from Pull Requests
item.description:
Terraform teams stopped deploying blind years ago. They open a pull request, a bot runs terraform plan and posts the result as a comment, a colleague reads exactly what will be created, changed and destroyed, and only then does anyone type atlantis apply. Most Bicep teams still merge and find out. The pipeline runs, the deployment succeeds or fails, and the first time anyone sees what Azure actually did is in the activity log afterwards.

That gap is why we built bicep-action. It is a pair of GitHub actions and an Azure DevOps pipeline that run Bicep the way Atlantis runs Terraform. Every change is planned in the pull request, the plan is reviewed by people, and only the approved plan is deployed. GitHub and Azure DevOps run the same shell scripts and post the same pull request comments, so a team can move between the two platforms without relearning anything.

It is free. The code and documentation are published under the BSD 3-Clause licence in a public repository, innofactororg/bicep-action, and you can pin it, fork it or read every line of it. It is also not a weekend project. The first commit was in November 2023, it has shipped fifteen releases since, and it is the mandated pipeline for every Bicep workload repository in one of the larger managed Azure estates we run, on Azure DevOps, as well as the pipeline behind the workloads our subscription-vending engine creates. Every fix in this week’s release, v2026.11.13, came from something a production pipeline hit.

This post walks through what it does, how it compares with Atlantis, and how to run it for one environment or for several.

What happens when you open a pull request

The flow has two jobs and a person in between.

The plan job only reads from Azure. It compiles the template, validates it, asks Azure what the deployment would change, runs the quality checks, and posts everything as one comment on the pull request. Any failed check fails the plan, and the deployment never starts.

The approval step uses what each platform already has. On GitHub it is an environment with required reviewers; on Azure DevOps it is an environment with an approval check. There is no bespoke approval mechanism to learn or secure.

The deploy job runs only after a successful plan and an approval. It deploys, comments the result on the same pull request, and on GitHub can turn on auto merge, so the branch is merged the moment the deployment succeeds. Main stays a record of what is actually deployed, which is the same property Atlantis users rely on.

What the plan checks

A plan is more than a what-if. The plan job runs a sequence of gates, each of which can fail the plan:

Step What it checks Fails the plan when
Bicep build The template and .bicepparam compile with the latest Bicep release It does not compile
Validate az deployment <scope> validate, and which resource providers the template needs Azure rejects the template
What-if What Azure would create, modify or delete; with stacks, what it would detach or delete The what-if fails, or a stack would delete something not approved
PSRule (opt-in) PSRule for Azure against the Well-Architected rules A rule fails
Cost estimate The monthly cost of the compiled template It exceeds your threshold
Bicep snapshot (automatic) The template against a committed snapshot of every resource it produces The template no longer matches the snapshot

The what-if is the heart of the comment. It is posted as a coloured diff, + for create, - for delete, ! for modify, with property-level changes listed under each resource and long results folded away. Reviewers read infrastructure changes the way they read code changes.

Deletes are approved in a commit, not discovered afterwards

The single most valuable thing bicep-action does is make deletes visible and deliberate. With deployment_mode: stack, the template is deployed as an Azure deployment stack, which means Azure knows which resources belong to the template. When you remove something from the code, the stack what-if shows exactly what would be detached or deleted.

The default behaviour for removed resources, detachAll, never deletes anything; the resource is simply released from the stack. If you choose deleteResources or deleteAll, a delete gate applies: the plan fails unless every resource the stack would delete is listed, by resource ID, in an approved-deletes file in the repository. Deleting a production resource therefore needs a reviewed commit that names it. If Azure cannot determine every resource that might be deleted, because some names are only known at deploy time, the plan fails rather than risk a hidden delete.

A snapshot that puts the real change in the diff

Bicep can now produce a snapshot: a fully expanded list of every resource the template produces, computed offline. Commit it next to your parameters file and the plan compares the template with it. If the template’s output changes, the plan fails until you regenerate and commit the snapshot, at which point the exact resource-level change sits in the pull request diff. A refactor that claims to change nothing can prove it. A Bicep release that silently changes compiled output gets reviewed like any other change.

Cost before you spend it

The plan runs the Azure Cost Estimator against the compiled template and puts the monthly estimate in the comment. Set a cost_threshold and the plan fails when the estimate exceeds it, or when the estimate cannot be made, because a budget you cannot check is not a budget. Leave it at the default and the estimate is report-only.

Deploy exactly what was planned

A reviewer approves a specific plan. If the deployment can drift from that plan, the review is worth very little. bicep-action closes the obvious gaps:

  • The same Bicep version. The plan records the Bicep CLI version it compiled with. The deploy job installs that version, even if a newer one shipped while the plan waited for approval.
  • The same mode and stack settings. The plan records its deployment mode and stack settings, and a deployment with different settings fails and asks for a new plan.
  • Deletes checked again. With a delete mode, the deploy job runs the delete gate again against the current state, immediately before deploying, because a plan can be hours old.
  • Fresh state where it matters. Values read from Azure during planning, such as existing tag values, are read again at deploy time rather than reused.

On Azure DevOps the deploy stage picks these values up from the plan stage automatically. On GitHub you pass the plan action’s outputs to the deploy action, which every example in the repository already does.

How it compares with Atlantis

bicep-action exists because Atlantis is right about the workflow. The comparison is worth making honestly, because the platforms are different in ways that matter.

Atlantis bicep-action
Language Terraform and OpenTofu Azure Bicep (and ARM JSON)
Where it runs A self-hosted server that receives webhooks Inside your existing GitHub Actions or Azure DevOps runners; nothing to host
Plan terraform plan, posted as a comment Build, validate, what-if, PSRule, cost and snapshot, posted as one comment
Apply trigger An atlantis apply comment, subject to apply requirements An environment approval in the platform’s own UI
Plan equals apply Applies the saved plan file No saved plan exists in ARM; the Bicep version and settings are pinned and deletes are re-checked
Locking Per project or directory, held until the pull request merges or is unlocked A concurrency group per Azure target on GitHub; one run at a time, deployments never cancelled
Policy Conftest/OPA policy checks PSRule for Azure, with your own baseline and rules
Cost Not built in Azure Cost Estimator, with an optional failing threshold
Deletes Shown as destroys in the plan Stack what-if plus a delete gate that requires approved IDs
Licence Apache 2.0 BSD 3-Clause

Two rows deserve a closer look.

Plan equals apply. Atlantis applies the exact plan file it showed you, which is the strongest guarantee available. ARM has no equivalent: a what-if is a preview, not a contract, and Azure re-evaluates the template at deployment time. bicep-action gets as close as the platform allows by pinning the compiler and settings and re-running the delete gate, but if something in Azure changes between plan and deploy, the deployment acts on the new state. Treat an old plan with suspicion, and re-plan when in doubt.

No server. Atlantis is a long-running service with credentials, a webhook endpoint and its own user interface, and it has to be patched, scaled and secured like any other. bicep-action has no running component. Credentials are your platform’s own workload identity federation or service connection, approvals are your platform’s environments, logs are your platform’s artifacts. The attack surface is the one you already have.

The lock deserves a note too. On GitHub, each example puts the workflow in a concurrency group per Azure target with cancel-in-progress: false. A second pull request waits until the first is deployed or rejected, so a deployment never runs over changes it did not plan. GitHub keeps one waiting run per group, so a newer waiting run replaces an older one, which is usually what you want.

The details that usually break pipelines

A few features exist because production pipelines kept tripping over the same things.

New subscriptions. A pipeline that runs against a subscription created minutes earlier, which is exactly what subscription vending produces, often cannot see it yet, or its role assignments have not propagated. The scripts retry that one error, the subscription not being visible, for up to subscription_wait_minutes (30 by default), logging what the identity can see on each attempt. Any other error, such as a missing permission, still fails at once. In real runs we have watched that window last more than an hour.

Tags that should keep their first value. Tags such as createdOn are meant to record when a resource was first deployed, but a template that sets them overwrites them on every run. The existing tags feature reads chosen tag values from the resources already in Azure, scoped to the resource groups you name, and passes them into the template so they survive redeployment.

Automation on top of the plan. Every plan writes whatif-summary.json: counts of creates, modifies, deletes, detaches and unsupported changes, the IDs involved, and whether the result was deterministic. One of the examples uses it to auto-approve plans that are provably safe, such as a plan with no deletes, no detaches, no unsupported changes and a deterministic result, and routes everything else to a human.

Secrets in the comment. Azure masks secret values in the what-if. This week’s release makes sure those masked values render correctly in Azure DevOps comments, where a run of asterisks used to turn the rest of the what-if into an unreadable block of comment colouring. It is a small fix, and a good example of why the project moves the way it does: it came from a reviewer struggling to read a real production plan.

One environment

On GitHub, a single-environment setup is a plan job and a deploy job. The plan:

yaml ShowHide 12 lines ⌄ 
- uses: actions/checkout@v7
- id: plan
  uses: innofactororg/bicep-action/.github/actions/plan@v1
  with:
    azure_client_id: ${{ env.azure_client_id }}
    azure_subscription_id: ${{ env.azure_subscription_id }}
    azure_tenant_id: ${{ env.azure_tenant_id }}
    deployment_mode: stack
    location: westeurope
    scope: sub
    template: infra/main.bicep
    template_parameters: infra/main.bicepparam

The deploy job runs in a GitHub environment with required reviewers and passes the plan’s outputs, providers, bicep_version and stack_settings, to the deploy action. The recommended.yml example in the repository is the complete version, with OpenID Connect sign-in, the concurrency lock, auto merge and the optional checks turned on.

On Azure DevOps, copy ms.azure.deploy.yml into the repository, set its variables, point an environment with an approval check at it, and add a build validation branch policy so it runs on every pull request. Every step is inline, so the single-environment pipeline needs no template repository. The pipeline downloads the scripts at the release you pin in WORKFLOW_VERSION.

Many environments

Real workloads have test and production, often more, each in its own subscription. bicep-action handles that by repeating the plan-and-deploy pair per environment and chaining them.

On GitHub, the multi-environment example runs test first and production second, all from one pull request:

text ShowHide 1 line ⌄ 
plan_test → deploy_test (environment: test) → plan_prod → deploy_prod (environment: production)

Each environment has its own subscription, parameters file (main.test.bicepparam, main.prod.bicepparam), stack name, cost threshold, GitHub environment with its own reviewers and federated credential, and artifact_identifier, so the logs of the two runs do not collide. Production is planned only after test has deployed, so the production plan reflects a change that has already been proven once, and only the production deploy merges the pull request.

On Azure DevOps, the repository ships reusable stage templates, plan-stage.yml and deploy-stage.yml. A multi-environment pipeline references the bicep-action repository as a resource, pinned to a release tag, and calls the templates once per environment with that environment’s variables:

yaml ShowHide 33 lines ⌄ 
resources:
  repositories:
    - repository: bicep_action
      type: github
      name: innofactororg/bicep-action
      ref: refs/tags/v1
      endpoint: github_connection

stages:
  - template: .azuredevops/templates/plan-stage.yml@bicep_action
    parameters:
      stageName: Plan_test
      serviceConnection: test_arm_connection
      variables:
        ARTIFACT_IDENTIFIER: test
        SUBSCRIPTION_ID: 11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111
        IN_TEMPLATE_PARAMS: infra/main.test.bicepparam
        STACK_NAME: app-test

  - template: .azuredevops/templates/deploy-stage.yml@bicep_action
    parameters:
      stageName: Deploy_test
      dependsOn: [Plan_test]
      planStageName: Plan_test
      environmentName: test
      serviceConnection: test_arm_connection
      variables:
        ARTIFACT_IDENTIFIER: test
        SUBSCRIPTION_ID: 11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111
        IN_TEMPLATE_PARAMS: infra/main.test.bicepparam
        STACK_NAME: app-test

  # ...then Plan_prod and Deploy_prod the same way, with the production values

Shared settings live in pipeline variables or a variable group, and per-environment values in each stage’s variables, which take precedence. Each environment gets its own service connection and its own approval check, so production reviewers approve production and nobody else.

Getting started

The repository has everything needed to adopt it, written to be copied rather than interpreted:

  • How it works: the plan and deploy jobs step by step, stacks and the delete gate, the snapshot, cost, PSRule and the summary file.
  • Configuration reference: every GitHub input and its Azure DevOps variable side by side, with defaults and recommended settings.
  • Setup guides for GitHub and Azure DevOps: environments, federated credentials, roles and branch policies.
  • Examples: recommended, minimal, multi-environment and auto-approval workflows for GitHub, and multi-environment and variable-group pipelines for Azure DevOps.
  • Troubleshooting: the messages you might see and what to do about them.

Pin a release: @v1 on GitHub and WORKFLOW_VERSION: v1 on Azure DevOps follow the latest release, or pin a dated tag such as v2026.11.13 if you want to choose when to move.

If you run Bicep in production and nobody reads what it will do before it does it, this is the cheapest fix you will find. It costs nothing, it runs in the CI you already have, and the first pull request it plans will show you something you did not know your template was about to change.

item.title: Azure Quota Groups: Recycling Capacity You Already Own
item.description:
The most expensive vCPU in Azure is the one you already had approved, gave back by accident, and now have to ask for again. That is exactly what happens every time an old subscription is cancelled. Years of quota increases, each one a support ticket, a business justification and a few days of waiting, disappear with the subscription. Meanwhile the brand-new subscription that replaces it starts life with default limits, in a region where capacity is tight, and the first deployment into it fails with a quota error the platform team then has to chase.

For most of Azure’s history there was no way around this. Quota was a property of the subscription: granted to it, enforced on it, and lost with it. Azure Quota Groups change that. They lift compute quota from the subscription to a group object, so quota can be pooled across subscriptions, handed back to the pool when a workload shrinks or is retired, and handed out again to a new subscription without a ticket.

I spend a lot of my time on landing zones and on subscription vending, the automated process that creates a subscription, places it in the management group hierarchy, wires it to the network and hands it to a team with a working deployment pipeline. In our case that engine is called Concierge. When a reviewer asked recently whether we should be putting every new subscription into a quota group as part of vending, especially as older subscriptions are being decommissioned, it was the right question, and working through the answer properly is what this post is about.

Quota Groups fit the problem well. They are also more subtle than the announcement suggests, and three limits decide whether you can use them at all. They only accept Enterprise Agreement and Microsoft Customer Agreement subscriptions, which rules out anything bought through a Cloud Solution Provider. They only cover IaaS compute quota, the vCPU limits per VM family. And they do nothing for region or zone access, which is a separate gate that fails in a confusingly similar way. If you run vending through a CSP partner, the first of those ends the conversation before it starts, and you need a different design.

First, what quota actually is, because everything after depends on it.

Quota, capacity and access are three different gates

When a deployment fails to get compute in Azure, it is usually one of three things, and they are often confused.

Quota is a limit Azure enforces on your subscription: how many vCPUs of a given VM family you may run in a given region, plus a total regional vCPU limit across families. It is a number on your subscription, it is checked at deployment time, and exceeding it fails the deployment with a quota error such as QuotaExceeded or an OperationNotAllowed that names the family and the limit. Quota is not capacity. A high limit does not mean the hardware is free; it means Azure has agreed you may use up to that much.

Capacity is whether the region actually has the hardware to place your VM right now. When it does not, you get an allocation failure such as AllocationFailed or ZonalAllocationFailed, even with plenty of quota. Quota increase requests are themselves checked against capacity, which is why increases in busy regions can be rejected or take a long time.

Access is whether your subscription may use a region, a zone or a VM size at all. Some regions are reserved and need an explicit access request. Within an open region, a specific size can be restricted for a specific subscription, which you can see in the SKU list: az vm list-skus --location <region> --size <size> --all returns a restrictions block, with a type of Location or Zone and a reasonCode of NotAvailableForSubscription. A deployment that hits it fails with SkuNotAvailable.

Quota Groups address the first gate only. Microsoft says so plainly in the documentation: “Quota Groups addresses the quota management pain point, it does not address the regional and or zonal access pain point.” Keep that sentence in mind, because it comes back when we get to automation.

What a quota group actually is

A quota group is an Azure Resource Manager object of type Microsoft.Quota/groupQuotas. It is created at a management group scope and inherits its permissions from that management group, but it is not tied to the hierarchy beneath it. Membership is explicit: you add subscriptions to it through the API, from any management group, and nothing is synchronised automatically. A subscription can belong to one quota group at a time.

Creating one is a single PUT:

http ShowHide 7 lines ⌄ 
PUT https://management.azure.com/providers/Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/{mgId}/providers/Microsoft.Quota/groupQuotas/{groupName}?api-version=2025-03-01

{
  "properties": {
    "displayName": "platform-compute-pool"
  }
}

Adding a subscription is another PUT, with no body:

http ShowHide 1 line ⌄ 
PUT https://management.azure.com/providers/Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/{mgId}/providers/Microsoft.Quota/groupQuotas/{groupName}/subscriptions/{subscriptionId}?api-version=2025-03-01

Both return provisioningState: ACCEPTED and complete asynchronously, so any automation has to poll before it moves on.

Two prerequisites catch people out. Every member subscription needs the Microsoft.Quota and Microsoft.Compute resource providers registered before it is added. And the roles are split across two scopes: GroupQuota Request Operator on the management group that holds the group, to create it and manage its limit, and Quota Request Operator on each participating subscription, to move quota in and out of it.

The group limit starts at zero

A new quota group has a limit of zero, and that surprises most people. Adding subscriptions does not change that. The documentation is explicit: “When added to the group, subscriptions carry their existing quota and usage. The subscriptions’ quota isn’t manipulated when added to a group. Subscription quota remains separate from the group limit.”

So the group limit is its own pot, separate from the members’ limits, and you fill it in one of two ways:

  1. Deallocation. You move unused quota from a member subscription into the group.
  2. A group limit increase. You ask Microsoft for more quota at the group level, for one region and one VM family at a time. It goes through the same capacity checks as a subscription request, and if it is rejected you fall back to a support ticket raised from the quota group blade. If it is approved, the quota is stamped on the group rather than on any one subscription.

Deployments still check the subscription

The other thing to internalise is where the check happens. The documentation says: “When deploying resources the quota check at runtime is done against the subscription quota.” The group is never consulted when you deploy. Quota in the group is inventory; it does nothing until you allocate it to a subscription.

That single fact shapes every automated flow. Putting a new subscription into a group gives it nothing. Somebody, or something, has to move quota from the group to the subscription before the first deployment, or that deployment fails exactly as it would have without a group.

Allocation and deallocation are absolute, not deltas

Moving quota in either direction uses the same call, and the semantics are easy to get wrong. You PATCH the subscription’s allocation for a region, and you set the new absolute limit you want the subscription to have, not the amount to move.

http ShowHide 14 lines ⌄ 
PATCH https://management.azure.com/providers/Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/{mgId}/subscriptions/{subscriptionId}/providers/Microsoft.Quota/groupQuotas/{groupName}/resourceProviders/Microsoft.Compute/quotaAllocations/{location}?api-version=2025-03-01

{
  "properties": {
    "value": [
      {
        "properties": {
          "resourceName": "standardddv4family",
          "limit": 50
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}

If the subscription currently has 60 vCPUs of that family, setting 50 deallocates 10 to the group. If it has 40, setting 50 allocates 10 from the group. The direction is implied by the difference between the current limit and the one you send.

Two constraints follow from that. You cannot deallocate below what the subscription is using, so quota is only reclaimable once the VMs consuming it are gone. And you cannot allocate more than the group has available.

Reading the state back is where the vocabulary matters. The allocation snapshot for a subscription returns its limit and a shareableQuota; a value of -10 means that subscription has given 10 vCPUs to the group. The group’s own view, from groupQuotaLimits/{location}, returns three numbers that are easy to conflate:

  • limit is what has been stamped on the group by approved increase requests.
  • availableLimit is what the group can hand out right now, including quota deallocated from members.
  • allocatedToSubscriptions lists each member’s net movement, negative for subscriptions that have given quota back.

In the documentation’s own example, a group with a stamped limit of 40 shows an availableLimit of 50, because a member had already deallocated 10. If you build reporting or automation on top of this API, availableLimit is the number that answers “can I allocate this?”.

Recycling quota from decommissioned environments

Decommissioning is the scenario that prompted the question, and it is where Quota Groups pay for themselves. Most estates that have been in Azure for a while are carrying subscriptions that are being consolidated or retired: old per-environment subscriptions, a previous generation of landing zone, workloads moving to a new hierarchy. Each one holds quota that somebody fought for.

The decommissioning flow with a quota group looks like this:

The order matters, and it is the order most decommissioning runbooks get wrong if they were written before quota groups existed.

  1. Join the old subscription to the group first. A subscription that is not a member cannot deallocate into it. If your retiring subscriptions predate the group, adding them is step zero.
  2. Remove the workloads. Deallocation cannot go below usage, so the VMs, scale sets and anything else consuming the family have to be gone first.
  3. Deallocate per region and per family. Set each allocation to the remaining usage, normally zero. This is one PATCH per region, with one entry per family in the body. Check shareableQuota afterwards.
  4. Remove the subscription from the group. On removal, “subscriptions carry their existing quota and usage. The group limit isn’t manipulated based on subscription removal.” Quota already deallocated stays in the pool.
  5. Only then cancel the subscription. Cancel first and the quota goes with it, which is exactly what you were trying to avoid.

Done in this order, a retirement programme becomes a quota source rather than a quota sink. Every subscription you close tops up the pool that the next one draws from, and the support tickets you raised years ago keep paying out.

One governance point is easy to miss. Deleting the management group that holds a quota group loses access to its limit, recoverable only by recreating a management group with the same ID. If you are reshaping your hierarchy at the same time as retiring subscriptions, which is common, put the quota group on a management group that is not going anywhere. A dedicated platform management group near the root is a better home than a landing-zone group that might be renamed or collapsed.

How it would fit an automated vending flow

A subscription-vending engine like Concierge runs a fixed sequence for every order: create the subscription, place it in the right management group, allocate its address space, create its repository and pipeline, give its deployment identity the access it needs, and hand over. The first deployment is the workload’s own pipeline, running as its own identity. That is deliberate, because the first run is the proof that the pipeline works. It also means that if the subscription lacks the quota the workload needs, the order is reported as complete and then the very first thing the team does fails.

With a quota group available, the vending flow gains one step between placement and handover:

A few design decisions fall out of building this rather than drawing it.

The order has to say what quota it needs. The engine cannot guess. The cleanest place for that is the architype, the template a workload is built from, which already knows its VM families and sizes. The order then carries region, family and vCPU count, with the architype supplying defaults.

The engine allocates; it does not manage the pool. Allocating from the group on behalf of a new subscription is a vending concern. Raising the group limit, deciding how much headroom to hold, and deallocating from retiring subscriptions are platform-ownership concerns. Mixing them gives an automated service the power to drain a pool that other teams depend on. In our design, the engine reads availableLimit, allocates if it can, and otherwise reports the shortfall rather than escalating on its own.

“Done, quota pending” is a real state. Increase requests are asynchronous and can be rejected. The order should be able to complete with an explicit warning and the request ID, so nobody runs the first deployment into a known shortfall and nobody believes a subscription is ready when it is not.

The roles are a real expansion of trust. The vending identity needs Quota Request Operator on each subscription it creates, which is modest because it usually owns those subscriptions anyway. It also needs GroupQuota Request Operator on the management group that holds the group, which is a standing grant at management-group scope in the customer’s tenant. That deserves the same scrutiny as any other privileged grant, and it is another argument for a dedicated management group.

One group per tenant, configured per customer. The group lives under a management group in one tenant. A vending engine that serves several customers from one deployment needs the group ID as customer configuration, not as a global setting.

Whether you can build any of it depends on three limits.

The three limits that decide whether you can use it

Billing: no CSP

The documentation lists it as the first limitation: “Available only for Enterprise Agreement, Microsoft Customer Agreement (MCA), and Internal subscriptions.”

Subscriptions bought through a Cloud Solution Provider, the partner-led Azure Plan billed under a Microsoft Partner Agreement, are none of those. They cannot be added to a quota group. That is not a configuration gap you can engineer around; the API will not accept them.

This matters more than it sounds, because a large share of managed estates are CSP. A managed service provider vending subscriptions for customers through its partner tenant is creating exactly the subscriptions Quota Groups exclude. Concierge supports all three agreement types, EA, MCA and MPA, but where a customer is billed through CSP, the vending engine has nothing to join the new subscription to.

The useful nuance is that an estate can be mixed. If the subscriptions being retired are EA or MCA, a quota group can still pool quota between them while they are wound down, and allocate it to other EA or MCA subscriptions. What it cannot do is carry that quota across the billing boundary into new CSP subscriptions.

Scope: IaaS compute only

The second limitation is “Supports IaaS compute resources only.” The group APIs live under resourceProviders/Microsoft.Compute, and the unit is the VM family vCPU limit. That covers virtual machines and scale sets.

It does not cover the quota that, in my experience, blocks new workloads most often today: Azure OpenAI tokens per minute, App Service and Functions plans, Container Apps environments, database vCores, public IP addresses. Each of those has its own quota and its own request process, usually per subscription. A platform built on PaaS and AI services can adopt quota groups and still find that most of its first-deploy failures are untouched by them.

Access: not a quota problem

The third limitation causes the most confusion, because it fails in a way that looks like quota. Quota transfers and deployments “will fail unless regional and or zonal access is provided on the subscription.” A new subscription can be denied a reserved region, a zone, or a specific VM size, and no amount of quota in a group changes that. You can allocate 200 vCPUs of a family to a subscription and still have every deployment fail with SkuNotAvailable.

Access is fixed through the region access request process, which is a support request, not an API call. For reserved regions it is an “Other Requests” ticket listing the subscriptions, region and planned usage. An automated flow can detect the restriction up front by reading the SKU restrictions for the target region and sizes, and it should, because it is far cheaper to report “this subscription cannot use this size here” at vending time than to let the workload team discover it.

What we do instead when the subscriptions are CSP

Because Concierge vends CSP subscriptions for some customers, we recorded the decision in an architecture decision record rather than leaving it in a review thread. It comes down to the same three gates, handled without a pool.

Quota is part of the order. After placement, the engine registers the providers it needs, reads current usage and limits through the Microsoft.Quota API at subscription scope, and raises a per-subscription increase for any shortfall, for whatever resource type the architype declares, not only compute. The quota API addresses a subscription’s limits by scope, along the lines of /subscriptions/{id}/providers/Microsoft.Compute/locations/{region}/providers/Microsoft.Quota/quotas/{family}, and the same pattern covers other providers that publish their limits through it. Whether every provider accepts API increase requests on a CSP subscription, or some still need a ticket, is something we are verifying on a test subscription before we rely on it.

Access is checked, not assumed. The engine reads SKU restrictions for the target region and sizes and reports any NotAvailableForSubscription before handover, with the region access request listed as an action rather than buried in a failed pipeline run.

The outcome is recorded on the order. Granted, pending with a request ID, or rejected. The order can finish as “done, quota pending”, and the ticket that tracks it says so.

Quota groups stay as an option for EA and MCA customers. Where the customer’s configuration names a group, the engine joins the subscription and allocates compute from it instead of raising a per-subscription compute request. Everything that is not compute still goes through the per-subscription path.

It is less elegant than a single pool. It still turns a failed first deployment into a known state at vending time, which is the outcome that actually matters to the team receiving the subscription.

Where this leaves you

Quota Groups solve a real and old problem: quota you paid for in time and tickets no longer has to die with the subscription that held it. For EA and MCA estates, especially ones in the middle of consolidating or retiring subscriptions, the flow is worth building now. Join the retiring subscriptions, deallocate before you cancel, keep the group on a management group that will outlive your current hierarchy, and let vending allocate from the pool rather than raise tickets.

Go in with the boundaries clear, though. The group is inventory, not entitlement: the subscription is what gets checked, so allocation is a step, not a side effect. It covers VM families, not the PaaS and AI quota that increasingly gates new workloads. It does nothing for region or zone access. And if your subscriptions come through CSP, it is not available to you at all, so the design has to treat quota, capacity and access as explicit, per-subscription parts of every order.

That last point is the one I would carry into any vending design, pool or no pool. A subscription is not ready because it exists. It is ready when the first deployment of the workload it was built for can succeed, and quota and access are part of that definition.

item.title: Azure DevOps Wiki to a Corporate PDF
item.description:
The project documentation is in good shape. The team has been maintaining an Azure DevOps wiki, the architecture pages link to the detailed design, and the deployment instructions sit alongside the decisions that explain them.

Then comes the handover request: “Can you send us the design document as a PDF? Please use the company template.”

That is a reasonable request. The recipient might not have access to Azure DevOps. An architecture board may need a fixed version to review, or the customer may need to file the document in a records system. A wiki is useful for the people doing the work; a controlled document is useful for the people accepting it.

Copying the pages into Word gets the first document out of the door. It also creates another copy to maintain. At the next revision, someone has to work out what changed, paste it again, repair the formatting and check the page numbers.

I wanted to keep the Markdown as the source and make the formatted document a build output. The implementation is available in innofactororg/markdown2pdf. It includes an Azure DevOps pipeline and a GitHub Action, both using Pandoc and a LaTeX template to produce a PDF artifact.

This post walks through the Azure DevOps route, explains where the corporate formatting belongs, and shows how the underlying Pandoc commands fit together.

Give the wiki a publishing process

Consider a design document spread across several wiki pages: an overview, requirements, architecture, security and an operational handover. The team wants to keep editing those pages normally. At agreed points, it needs to publish those sections as one document with a cover, version history, contents page and consistent branding.

There are two separate decisions here: which content belongs in the document, and how that content should look. The workflow keeps them separate:

text ShowHide 10 lines ⌄ 
Markdown pages + explicit document order
                  |
                  v
Merge content and resolve supported asset paths
                  |
                  v
Apply document metadata, history and replacements
                  |
                  v
Pandoc + corporate LaTeX template -> PDF artifact

The order file defines the publication. The template defines its presentation. Authors can change the design without adjusting headers and footers on every page, while template changes can be reviewed independently of technical content.

The output is a snapshot of the source used by that build. Generating it does not approve it: the organisation’s review, sign-off and records process still applies.

Start with the Git repository behind the wiki

An Azure DevOps wiki is backed by Git, but the type of wiki matters when arranging the build.

A project wiki has its own wiki repository. Use the wiki’s Clone wiki option to obtain the repository URL, then clone it using your normal authenticated Git setup:

bash ShowHide 1 line ⌄ 
git clone <wiki-clone-url> wiki-source

Replace the placeholder; don’t put a personal access token into a command that will be saved in a script or build log.

A code wiki publishes Markdown from a normal repository and branch. That is a convenient arrangement when you want documentation changes reviewed through pull requests and built by a pipeline in the same repository.

The supplied conversion pipeline checks out self. It does not automatically discover or export a separate project wiki. For a project wiki, add an authenticated checkout or staging step to bring its Markdown and attachments into the build workspace, or deliberately move to a code-wiki arrangement. Keep that acquisition step explicit so that a successful build cannot quietly publish an outdated copy.

For the rest of this example, assume the Markdown is available in the pipeline’s source repository under docs/design.

Choose the document’s reading order

A wiki’s navigation tree is not necessarily a good printed document. It may include working notes, obsolete pages or several audiences’ material. Alphabetical file order is rarely what a design reviewer needs either.

The converter uses a document.order file to select the pages and their sequence:

text ShowHide 10 lines ⌄ 
docs/
  design/
    document.order
    Overview.md
    Requirements.md
    Architecture.md
    Security.md
    Operations.md
    images/
      architecture.png

For this document, docs/design/document.order contains:

text ShowHide 6 lines ⌄ 
# Customer design and handover
Overview.md
Requirements.md
Architecture.md
Security.md
Operations.md

Each entry names a file relative to the document folder, including its extension. Lines beginning with # are comments. Nested paths can be listed explicitly when the content spans subfolders.

Azure DevOps also uses .order files for wiki navigation. Those are not interchangeable with document.order: the converter expects an explicit list of Markdown paths, not a recursive walk of the wiki’s navigation files.

My early experiments used PowerShell helpers named Get-DocfxFolderItems, Get-DocfxItem and Invoke-DocfxTocProcessing to inspect the wiki hierarchy and its .order files. That was useful for exploring the source structure. The implementation shared here uses the simpler publication manifest instead; you don’t need those helpers or DocFX to run it.

This gives the author an editorial decision to review in Git. A new wiki page doesn’t become part of the customer deliverable merely because it exists.

Add the Azure DevOps pipeline

Copy the repository’s Azure DevOps pipeline into the source repository, for example as:

text ShowHide 1 line ⌄ 
.pipelines/docs.design.yml

Use the full supplied pipeline, not just the variable block below. For this scenario, its variables would look like this:

yaml ShowHide 14 lines ⌄ 
variables:
  FIRST_CHANGE_DESCRIPTION: Initial design draft
  FOLDER: docs/design
  GIT_LOG_LIMIT: 15
  HISTORY_FILE: history.txt
  MAIN_AUTHOR: Architecture Team
  ORDER_FILE: document.order
  OUT_FILE: solution-design.pdf
  PROJECT: CUSTOMER-001
  REPLACE_FILE: replace.json
  SKIP_GIT_COMMIT_HISTORY: false
  SUBTITLE: Solution Design and Operational Handover
  TITLE: Customer Platform
  WORKFLOW_VERSION: v3

The next sections define the optional history.txt and replace.json used here. Leave their variables empty if you don’t want those features.

FOLDER tells the converter where the content lives. ORDER_FILE selects the publication manifest. TITLE, SUBTITLE and PROJECT provide document metadata, while OUT_FILE names the PDF published as a pipeline artifact.

WORKFLOW_VERSION selects the converter scripts and template assets fetched from GitHub. The repository’s example uses v3. For a controlled publishing process, choose and review a specific version; use an immutable commit reference where your standards require it. A template change can alter the deliverable even when none of its Markdown changes.

The supplied pipeline performs these jobs:

  1. Checks out the source with fetchDepth: 0, making Git history available for the document history feature.
  2. Caches TeX Live and installs the conversion dependencies.
  3. Fetches the converter, LaTeX template and branding images from the selected implementation version.
  4. Runs the conversion with the configured inputs.
  5. Publishes the resulting PDF with PublishPipelineArtifact@1.

Create a pipeline in Azure DevOps using Existing Azure Pipelines YAML file, select the copied file, and run it manually for the first test. The agent needs access both to the source content and to the external locations used to download the tools and template.

For Azure Repos Git, configure build validation in the branch policies if you want the PDF generated during pull-request review. Don’t rely on the sample YAML’s pr: block to configure Azure Repos PR validation; the branch policy is the relevant control there. Configure a normal CI trigger separately if you also want builds after merges.

The finished PDF is a downloadable artifact on the run. Publishing it to SharePoint, a customer portal or a records system is a separate delivery step, with its own access and approval requirements.

Make the template match the document standard

The implementation has three main presentation assets:

  • tools/designdoc.tex: the LaTeX document template.
  • tools/designdoc-cover.png: the cover image.
  • tools/designdoc-logo.png: the page-header logo.

The template provides a title page, version history, table of contents and styled content pages. Headers carry the logo and document context; footers provide page numbering. The converter supplies metadata such as title, project, authors and date.

That is the place to implement the approved fonts, colours, margins and page furniture. Keep those choices out of individual Markdown pages so authors aren’t maintaining formatting instructions alongside the design.

The supplied assets are Innofactor-specific. To publish under another organisation’s standard, maintain a reviewed customisation or fork, and update the pipeline’s download locations to use it. Copying a different template into the documentation folder is not enough if the pipeline still fetches the upstream assets on every run.

Also inspect tools/convert.sh. Some presentation and policy values are supplied there rather than in the .tex file, including an Innofactor-specific confidentiality statement. Changing the logo alone does not make the document appropriate for another company or for public distribution.

A template can reproduce a corporate layout, but that does not automatically make a document compliant. If the standard requires a document identifier, classification, approver table or specific revision fields, add and review those explicitly. Check the generated PDF against an approved sample before treating the template as ready for formal use.

Decide what “version history” means

The converter supports three sources for the history page, in priority order:

  1. An explicit history file, when supplied and found.
  2. The fallback author and initial change description when Git history is deliberately skipped.
  3. Git commit history for the documentation folder, falling back to the initial entry when no history is available.

Git history is useful during drafting, but commit messages are not always suitable for a customer-facing revision table. “Fix typo” and “move diagram again” record the work without describing a formal issue of the document.

For a controlled deliverable, I would use docs/design/history.txt:

text ShowHide 2 lines ⌄ 
1.0|Oct 26, 2023|Architecture Team|Initial design issued for review
1.1|Oct 28, 2023|Architecture Team|Updated network design following review

The format is Version|Date|Author|Description, one entry per line, without a header row. These are illustrative entries, not dates generated by the pipeline.

Set HISTORY_FILE: history.txt to use it. If you prefer Git-derived history during development, leave that setting empty, keep SKIP_GIT_COMMIT_HISTORY: false, and use GIT_LOG_LIMIT to bound the number of entries.

Neither option proves that a revision was approved. Record approval through the process your organisation actually uses, and retain the issued PDF with its source revision and build reference.

Reuse content without maintaining customer-specific copies

A common documentation problem is a largely reusable design with a few customer-specific names. The converter’s replacement file lets the publishing step substitute those values.

For example, a Markdown paragraph might contain:

markdown ShowHide 1 line ⌄ 
The primary services for {organization name} run in {data center name}.

With docs/design/replace.json:

json ShowHide 4 lines ⌄ 
{
  "{organization name}": "Contoso",
  "{data center name}": "WE1"
}

Set REPLACE_FILE: replace.json to apply the replacements to the merged content before conversion. Keep that configuration with the publication so reviewers can see which values were used.

This is simple text substitution, not a full document templating language. The implementation uses shell and sed processing, so test values containing slashes, ampersands or other special characters before relying on them. Don’t use the file as a secret store; the substituted text is going into a distributed document.

Write Markdown that survives the move to paper

A browser can scroll horizontally. A portrait A4 page cannot. A few authoring habits make the generated PDF much more useful.

Keep tables narrow, give diagrams readable labels, and split large comparison matrices into smaller sections. Use proper Markdown headings rather than formatting ordinary paragraphs to resemble headings. Let the generated contents page describe the document instead of carrying a wiki-specific contents widget into print.

Use explicit relative image paths where possible:

markdown ShowHide 1 line ⌄ 
![Platform architecture](./images/architecture.png)

The converter rewrites supported relative paths as it merges pages, and the repository specifically recommends paths starting with ./. It is not a complete Azure DevOps wiki-rendering engine. Check attachments, page links, anchors and any wiki-specific syntax against the output. Turning a path into an absolute build-agent path does not make it a useful link for the recipient of a PDF.

The implementation also supports fenced admonitions through its Pandoc filter:

markdown ShowHide 3 lines ⌄ 
::: warning
Confirm the recovery procedure before scheduling the production cutover.
:::

The supported classes are warning, important, note, caution and tip. Check how these appear in both your wiki and PDF; support in the converter does not guarantee identical rendering in every Markdown viewer.

The supplied template is designed for portrait A4 and does not offer a per-page landscape switch. Wide tables and diagrams need an editorial decision, not just a smaller font. Section numbering is not enabled automatically by the supplied conversion command either; agree a consistent approach before numbering headings manually.

Where the original Pandoc commands fit

The pipeline wraps tools that can also be used directly. These commands are useful for understanding the conversion or testing a formatting change without first wiring up a complete publishing process.

Combine pages in an explicit order

Pandoc can read an ordered list of inputs from a defaults file. For example, save this as defaults.yaml:

yaml ShowHide 5 lines ⌄ 
input-files:
  - Overview.md
  - Requirements.md
  - Architecture.md
verbosity: INFO

Then run Pandoc from the folder containing those files:

bash ShowHide 1 line ⌄ 
pandoc --defaults defaults.yaml -o output.docx

This illustrates the same principle as document.order, but the formats are different. defaults.yaml is Pandoc configuration; document.order is input to the repository’s merge script. They are not two files you must maintain for the supplied pipeline.

Defaults files can also hold resource paths and other conversion settings. Pandoc supports ${.} in path-valued fields to refer to the defaults file’s directory, which helps when keeping configuration and supporting assets together. See the Pandoc defaults documentation for the available fields.

Use a Word reference document when Word is the deliverable

Sometimes the official handover format is DOCX, or the recipient needs to make tracked edits. Pandoc’s Word route uses a reference document:

bash ShowHide 1 line ⌄ 
pandoc --defaults defaults.yaml --reference-doc=reference.docx -o output.docx

Save the approved template as a .docx, rather than passing a .dotx directly. Put reference.docx in the working folder or pass its explicit path.

Pandoc uses the reference document’s styles and document properties; it does not fill an arbitrary existing Word document as though it were a mail-merge template. Check the result against the corporate standard, especially when it contains custom cover content or mandatory tables.

This is a separate output route. The markdown2pdf implementation described above renders through LaTeX and XeLaTeX; it does not take a corporate Word template and automatically turn that into its PDF layout.

Apply LaTeX settings to the PDF route

For local PDF experiments, a header include such as head.tex can hold page and link settings:

tex ShowHide 9 lines ⌄ 
\usepackage{fancyvrb,newverbs}
\usepackage[top=2cm, bottom=1.5cm, left=2cm, right=2cm]{geometry}
\hypersetup{
    bookmarksopen=true,
    colorlinks=true,
    linkcolor=blue,
    filecolor=magenta,
    urlcolor=blue
}

Apply it when generating a PDF:

bash ShowHide 1 line ⌄ 
pandoc --defaults defaults.yaml --pdf-engine=xelatex -H head.tex -o output.pdf

This requires Pandoc and a suitable TeX installation. A LaTeX header does not style DOCX output; use the reference document for that. In the automated implementation, make the equivalent changes in the reviewed template and metadata rather than maintaining a competing set of local overrides.

Inspect code highlighting and link colours

Pandoc can list its syntax-highlighting styles and recognised languages:

bash ShowHide 2 lines ⌄ 
pandoc --list-highlight-styles
pandoc --list-highlight-languages

For a standalone experiment using its built-in highlighting:

bash ShowHide 1 line ⌄ 
pandoc --pdf-engine=xelatex --highlight-style zenburn test.md -o test.pdf

Or combine the defaults file with numbered sections and a different highlight style:

bash ShowHide 2 lines ⌄ 
pandoc --defaults defaults.yaml --pdf-engine=xelatex -H head.tex \
  -N --highlight-style=espresso -V colorlinks -o output.pdf

Language labels on fenced code blocks help Pandoc choose the right syntax rules. The shared converter uses --listings, so its code presentation is controlled through the LaTeX listings configuration; changing a --highlight-style example is not the same as changing that pipeline’s code styling.

Link colours can be tested independently too:

bash ShowHide 2 lines ⌄ 
pandoc --pdf-engine=xelatex -V colorlinks -V urlcolor=blue \
  -V toccolor=red test.md -o test.pdf

The text must be recognised as a link. Use Markdown links or an explicit autolink such as <https://example.com> rather than assuming that every URL-looking string will become one.

These commands explain the building blocks. For repeated delivery, the versioned pipeline should remain the publishing route, so the document doesn’t depend on whichever combination of flags someone last used locally.

Review the artifact before issuing it

For the first run, choose a small but representative document: several pages, an image, a table and a code block. Inspect the PDF rather than treating a green pipeline result as evidence of document quality.

Check that the pages appear in the intended order, images resolve, table columns fit and code is legible. Confirm that the cover, history, confidentiality text and branding are appropriate for the recipient. Test links from the downloaded PDF, outside the build agent and ideally without access to the source wiki.

After that first review, the publishing loop becomes manageable: edit the Markdown, review the change, build the PDF and retain the version that was actually issued. If you want artifacts on every relevant change, include order files, history files, replacement files and pipeline configuration in your trigger or branch-policy path filters, not just .md files.

Use the implementation

The complete project is available at innofactororg/markdown2pdf, with Azure DevOps setup instructions and a GitHub Action example for documentation hosted on GitHub. The code and documentation are released under the BSD 3-Clause License; retain the relevant notices when adapting them.

The useful starting point is one document, one explicit order file and one reviewed template. Keep the wiki as the place the team works, and publish a PDF from the reviewed source when someone needs a formal copy. The next revision can then follow the same process without rebuilding the document by hand in Word.

  • markdown2pdf source and usage
  • Azure DevOps pipeline implementation
  • Conversion script
  • Pandoc user guide
  • Converting Markdown to Beautiful PDF with Pandoc — jdhao

item.title: Running Tailscale on a Ubiquiti EdgeRouter X
item.description:
Having grown up in the world of ‘on premise’ computing, I have always prioritized data privacy in my home network.

Though there may not be much of interest to hackers, there is still personal data and services that I want to keep secure. I have spent years working with OpenVPN and IPSec, building and supporting a Dynamic Multi-site VPN Mesh with Cisco DMVPN, and I know first hand the challenges of connecting clients to a private network and managing keys.

When WireGuard emerged a few years ago, I quickly switched to an Edge Router X to make it my default VPN technology. Though WireGuard had some scaling challenges to manage, it was still significantly easier to use than what I was used to.

Then Tailscale came along, which made WireGuard even more user-friendly with additional security features like key rotation and single sign-on. While I’ve been using Tailscale on all of my systems, including Linux, macOS, and iOS, I recently decided to shift the endpoint to the edge of my network to make connectivity even easier.

My EdgeRouter passed away, it served me well, and has been replaced by a UniFi Cloud Gateway Max, And is quite happy to assume the tailscale responsibility

Latest builds now support the tailscale update command, which makes the maintenance trivial. Removed defunct configuration details from the post

Updating notes to reflect switch from Unstable which I have been using since verision 1.7, to the current stable branch running 1.38.

Updating notes to reflect switch from stable 1.40 to 1.50.

Ubuquiti Edge Router X

The router at the edge of my home network is currently a Ubiquiti EdgeRouter X, which boasts a power-efficient MIPSLE CPU and runs on a Linux-based operating system that was derived from VyattaOS.

The device offers a wide range of settings that can be adjusted via SSH that are not available through the web UI. With Tailscale, which provides MIPS binaries in addition to ARM, I can now connect the router to Tailscale and treat it like any other Linux system.

In this post, we’ll explore how to configure the EdgeRouter to function as a gateway, allowing external systems to access internal networks.

Installation and Upgrade

The Tailscale client comes in two branches, Tailscale Unstable and Tailscale Stable. While Unstable was necessary for me a few years ago, I now prefer using Stable. To download the latest version for the MIPS platform, visit the Tailscale Stable page and scroll down to find the current build, such as tailscale_1.54.0_mips.tgz.

To install and set up Tailscale, follow these steps:

  1. Navigate to your home folder and download the current build. Then, extract it and delete the download file:
shell ShowHide 4 lines ⌄ 
cd ~
curl https://pkgs.tailscale.com/stable/tailscale_1.54.0_mipsle.tgz -o tailscale.tgz  
tar xzvf tailscale.tgz  
rm tailscale.tgz
  1. Move the extracted files to their proper locations on the router and create the necessary directories for log data and runtime socket file:
shell ShowHide 18 lines ⌄ 
# Change into a real shell and switch to root user 
sudo bash 
    
# Navigate to the extracted download 
cd tailscale_1.50.0_mipsle 
    
# Move the application to the right location 
mv tailscale* /usr/sbin 
    
# Place systemd and defaults into etc 
mv systemd/tailscaled.service /etc/systemd/system 
mv systemd/tailscaled.defaults /etc/default/tailscaled 
    
# Create the state storage folders 
mkdir /var/lib/tailscale /run/tailscale

# Create a symbolic link from /usr/bin which is in the path
sudo ln -s /usr/sbin/tailscale /usr/bin/tailscale

Initial Confuration

The following steps are not typically required if you are upgrading between versions; however if this is a fresh installation you will need to start the service, and authenticate your node with the tailnet.

  1. Start it up! If you have any issues, they should appear here as the service gets started. Check the logs by tailing the output from Tailscale using tail -f /var/log/messages.
shell ShowHide 1 line ⌄ 
systemctl enable --now tailscaled
  1. Authenticate your device to Tailscale by starting it up and following the instructions. You can also use some options, such as:
    • --advertise-routes: a comma-separated list of subnets that other clients can reach via this router
    • --advertise-exit-node: allows any Tailscale instance to act as an exit node, sending your otherwise-public traffic to a specific node that will NAT your traffic out to the internet. This option is useful when you’re on an untrusted network or if you want to source your traffic from a different network.
shell ShowHide 1 line ⌄ 
tailscale up --advertise-routes=172.16.1.0/24 --advertise-exit-node --accept-routes
text ShowHide 24 lines ⌄ 

When you start Tailscale, it will present you with a URL to visit that allows you to authenticate the device to your Tailscale account. 
- ![](./sw.tailscale.configuration.authenticate.png)
- Once you do this, your router will show up under the “Machines” list in the admin UI
- ![](./sw.tailscale.configuration.tailscale-settings.png)

> [!Warning] Disconnect
> At this point all traffic on the router will appear to black hole for both ingress and egress. 
> To restore service, we must acknowledge the settings in the Tailscale portal; this may required that you use an alternate device that is not on this network to reach the port. Once in the portal we should validate and enable both settings we applied in the `tailscale up` command, which will then unblock the device
> ![](./sw.tailscale.configuration.device-configuration.png)


## Final Testing

If you’ve made it this far, you should be able to ping other Tailscale nodes bidirectionally.

If you’d like hosts behind the EdgeRouter to communicate to other Tailscale clients outside the local network, you’ll want to add a NAT so that traffic knows where to go (without one, you’ll only have inbound access to devices on the network). To do this, you can add it via CLI:

```shell
router$ configure
router# set service nat rule 5012 description Tailscale
router# set service nat rule 5012 outbound-interface tailscale0
router# set service nat rule 5012 protocol all
router# set service nat rule 5012 type masquerade

…or find it in the Ubiquiti web UI under “Firewall/NAT” and click a few options. The tailscale0 interface will not show up in the dropdown list, so you must choose “Other” and type in tailscale0.
